I covered a lot of ground above, is there something specific you would like me to focus on? The basic theory on how this works, or perhaps specific examples from it being applied in the real world?

I guess I would be curious to know about the risk. Laptops for example, are you not worried that there will not be a buyer for them and then they will rapidly become obsolete?

How do you go about locating a seller of these things? How do you deal with larger competition?

Hmm...okay...

Uhm.. There is always risk. You can get caught with inventory you cannot sell, or are forced to sell at a loss. That really is a function of being careful about what you buy. Also, locating sellers is difficult, especially because you are not the only one looking for them. Also, larger competition always exists, even for the largest players. It's like the weather, there is not much you can do about that.

With the laptops specifically, at the time I was doing that laptops were very expensive. New units typically started about $2000, and ranged upwards through $5000, or even $6000. This is 1990's money. Also, that was when everyone suddenly decided they needed to have a computer. This is before Windows 95 came out. At this time, if you looked in the Yellow pages, there was only a single page of listings for computer stores. Then the universities told the students everyone would be using a computer. Also, having a laptop was a status symbol, something only the richest students had.

So, the stores that did exist locally didn't have the kind of inventory to meet that demand. Thousands of local students wanted laptops. Also, students have money, but they are not exactly rich. They will spend for items they believe they have to have as part of their education.

What I did was to source the guys who were dumping used laptops into the market in Toronto. Many of those were corporate leasebacks. Say you have a bank. The bank equips their employees with the latest laptops fresh off the assembly lines from IBM. The banks get these models before they even reach the retail stores. However, the bank doesn't buy the laptops, they only lease them for between one to two years, after which they are returned to the leasing company, who then dumps them out on the after market for resale.

The banks upgrade to the latest new models on fresh leases, and guys like me would buy up the older models at very discounted prices. These deals are happening in batches of 10,000 units at a time. The leasing companies just hand them of to a liquidator for a bulk price, and he then breaks that down into smaller quantity sales over time. These guys own warehouses filled with all kinds of second hand stuff, in like new condition. If you have the money you can buy it by the pallet load. If you have enough to buy it by the container load, then what you really need is your own warehouse.

Consider also, at that time people did not know how to use the computers they were given. Many of the leasebacks were still sealed in the original shipping boxes and were not in fact ever used at all - so when I say like new, that is what I mean. This form of product distribution is called grey market, or after market - not for retail store shelves. Not for retail sale, and they don't come with retail warranties. Many do, however, retain their manufacturer factory warranties if they are new enough. Warranty service for one year was provided by my own self. If necessary, I could always just give them another book in a worst case scenario. Usually, I just fixed them myself. Parts are available for most major brands, and there are multiple sources for these as well.

In retail distribution, supply lines are restricted, and resellers have to be authorized to even get access to the product lines. This is done to artificially raise the prices. Do you really believe it costs $75,000 to build a car? Of course not. It probably costs less than $20,000 to build the $75,000 car. However, if you want the newest latest model, you can only buy it retail through the authorized dealer. Basically, you cannot get that any cheaper. What you can get is last year's model, used, in like new condition, from a wide variety of sources, and often at an excellent price.

Dealing with larger sellers is really a function of price. When retailers are gouging the market, like when they were selling notebooks for $4000 in 1993, and I could buy last year's model, still in the factory box, and sell it very profitably for $2000, with a one year no questions repair or replacement warranty, at a time when the economy was poor and everyone was hunting for bargains... well, like I said, I was doing this 10 times a day, every day. The phone never stopped ringing. I had waiting lists, and was often sold out of inventory.

That lasted for a while, however, by the year 2000, the yellow pages had 20 or 30 pages of computer sales related listings, the economy was booming, everyone had easy credit, the market was flooded with computers, dirt cheap and all of the profits were gone. i would say I had 3 to 4 very solid years, but after that the price competition really began in earnest. Products that wholesaled for $300 retailed for $325. Y2K was the last gasp of the computer retail age, and once that passed, everyone had a new computer and there were no new sales for months, so I closed my business. So did many others. Today the number of small retail outlets is almost back to zero. There is no excess money there to be had.

You see, the forces of free market competition inevitably fill in these market externalities. Anywhere someone is making money hand over fist will inevitably attract more competitors, and over time, increased competition drives down the prices and the profit margins. You have to go where the markets lead you. Right now, some of the hottest markets are in robotics and drone technology, for example. Soon enough, drones will be ubiquitous, mass produced, easy to use, and dirt cheap. New areas of high profitability are always opening up, and they are always temporary. Some last longer than others.

One very important lesson I learned about all this concerns how big a risk you are willing to take on any given deal. When you are buying you are essentially gambling on your assumed ability to move the product. The one fundamental rule is to never make a purchase so large that if your assumption should turn out to be wrong, you will then be out of business. You should always assume that you are going to be wrong, or that you are somehow going to get fucked on the deal. That way, when you make a mistake, you are still financially strong enough to survive it. You have to be able to eat the losses which will, sooner or later, occur.

Another aspect to consider is unmet demand. The best scenario is one where you can buy and resell immediately, because so many people want to buy, so badly, that they are willing to deal with a new or unknown seller. Take now for instance. We hear stories of ammunition shortages all over the place. Anyone right now with a supply of ammunition isn't going to have much trouble selling it. That is certainly not true in normal times, when ammo is sold everywhere and it is dirt cheap, and therefore not very profitable.

The point is you have to watch the markets and listen to the people. When they need something they cannot get, find it and bring it to them. Opportunities of this nature are nearly always temporary.
